diagnostic_evidence.quote: Therefore, there exists a direction $\bm a = (a_1, \ldots, a_m)^\top$ supported on $\text{supp}_{\delta}(\bm q^{*}_n)$ such that  $\sum_{i\in [m]}\frac{a_i}{\sigma^2(x_i)}R_iR^\top_i = 0$. Applying a perturbation argument for $\bm q^{*}_n$ along $\bm a$ yields another optimal solution that has a smaller $\delta$-support.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof establishes that if the support exceeds $n(n+1)/2$, the $n \times n$ symmetric matrices $R_i R_i^\top$ are linearly dependent, yielding coefficients $a_i$ such that $\sum_{i} \frac{a_i}{\sigma^2(x_i)} R_i R_i^\top = 0$. However, for the perturbed vector $\bm q_n^* + t\bm a$ to remain in the feasible set $\mathcal P_m(\delta)$, it must also satisfy the probability simplex constraint $\sum_{i=1}^m a_i = 0$. Adding this scalar linear constraint means that a non-zero perturbation direction $\bm a$ is only guaranteed to exist when $|\supp_\delta(\bm q_n^*)| > \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + 1$. Thus, the perturbation argument only proves that the support is at most $\frac{n^2+n}{2} + 1$, not $\frac{n^2+n}{2}$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Incorporate the linear constraint $\sum_{i=1}^m a_i = 0$ into the linear dependency argument and adjust the bound in the statement of Lemma 3.2 to $\frac{n^2+n}{2} + 1$.
issues.overall_effect: The exact upper bound on the number of points with allocation strictly greater than $\delta$ in Lemma 3.2 is off by 1.
issues.title: Sparsity bound in Lemma 3.2 neglects the simplex sum-to-one constraint
issues.why_classification: Relaxing the bound from $\frac{n^2+n}{2}$ to $\frac{n^2+n}{2} + 1$ is a local adjustment that preserves the order $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ sparsity guarantee and leaves all downstream results unaffected.

issues.failure_explanation: In part 2 of Theorem 4.1, the bound is stated with the unconditioned expectation $\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*)]$. In the proof, this is obtained via $\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*) \mid \AA] = \frac{\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*) \mathbb I_\AA]}{\P(\AA)} \leq 2\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*)]$. However, $H(\bm q_n^*) = \tr(\bm U(\bm q_n^*)^{-1})$ is only defined when $\bm W^{1/2}\bm V$ has full column rank (as assumed in Lemma 3.2). On $\AA^c$, $\bm W^{1/2}\bm V$ can be rank-deficient or singular, meaning $\bm q_n^*$ and $H(\bm q_n^*)$ are not well-defined and the unconditioned expectation $\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*)]$ can be infinite. Bounding $\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*) \mathbb I_\AA]$ by dropping $\mathbb I_\AA$ is invalid.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Retain the conditioning on $\AA$ in the bound, writing $\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*) \mid \AA]$ instead of $\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*)]$, in both Theorem 4.1 part 2 and Theorem 4.4.
issues.overall_effect: The error bound for the reweighted estimator in Theorem 4.1 (and its constrained counterpart Theorem 4.4) uses an ill-defined or potentially infinite unconditioned expectation instead of the conditioned expectation.
issues.title: Theorem 4.1 part 2 bounds conditional error by ill-defined unconditioned expectation
issues.why_classification: On the event $\AA$, $\bm W^{1/2}\bm V$ is well-conditioned by construction, so $\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*) \mid \AA]$ is finite and well-behaved. Keeping the conditioning on $\AA$ immediately resolves the defect without weakening any substantive guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Compared to \eqref{p1-1}, it improves the error dependence on the estimation variance at the cost of introducing a multiplicative constant in front of the approximation bias $\OPT$.

issues.failure_explanation: Remark 4.3 claims that $H(\bm p_n^*) \leq G(\bm p_n^*)$ by the Gauss-Markov theorem, which would imply $\E_\XX[H(\bm q_n^*)] \leq \E_\XX[G(\bm p_n^*)]$. This is mathematically false. The Gauss-Markov theorem bounds the covariance of WLS by that of OLS: $\Cov(\widehat{\bm\alpha}_{\text{WLS}}) \preceq \Cov(\widehat{\bm\alpha}_{\text{OLS}}) = (\bm X^\top\bm X)^{-1}\bm X^\top\bm\Sigma\bm X(\bm X^\top\bm X)^{-1}$, where $\bm X = \bm W^{1/2}\bm V$. The trace of this OLS covariance is not $G(\bm p) = \tr(\bm X^\top\bm\Sigma\bm X)$. When the singular values of $\bm X$ are strictly less than 1 (which can occur even on event $\AA$), $H(\bm p_n^*)$ strictly exceeds $G(\bm p_n^*)$ (for example, if $\bm X = c \bm I$ with $c < 1$, $H(\bm p) = c^{-2} \tr(\bm\Sigma) > c^2 \tr(\bm\Sigma) = G(\bm p)$). Therefore, the claim that HLS-2 provably improves the estimation variance over HLS-1 via $H(\bm p_n^*) \leq G(\bm p_n^*)$ is false.

failure_location.quote: so that $H(\bm q^{*}_n)\leq H(\bm p^*_n)\leq G(\bm p^*_n)$ (the first inequality follows from the definition of $ m q_n^*$ and the second uses the Gauss--Markov theorem), which implies $\E_\XX[H(\bm q^{*}_n)]\leq \E_\XX[G(\bm p^*_n)]$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Clarify that Gauss-Markov bounds $H(\bm p)$ by the trace of the OLS covariance, which on event $\AA$ satisfies $H(\bm p_n^*) \leq \|(\bm X^\top\bm X)^{-1}\|_2^2 G(\bm p_n^*) \leq (1/0.81^2) G(\bm p_n^*)$, rather than $H(\bm p_n^*) \leq G(\bm p_n^*)$, and qualify the variance reduction claim accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The prose assertion in Remark 4.3 that HLS-2 provably achieves lower estimation variance than HLS-1 is unsupported and mathematically false as stated.
issues.title: False claim that Gauss-Markov theorem implies reweighted variance is bounded by unweighted variance
issues.why_classification: On the conditioning event $\AA$, the OLS Gram matrix has eigenvalues in $[0.81, 1.21]$, meaning $H(\bm q_n^*)$ is bounded by a modest constant factor times $G(\bm p_n^*)$. Modifying the prose remark to include this factor corrects the statement without affecting the formal algorithms.
